analysis.one_liner: Taxes fortunes above $50 million at 2%, and above $1 billion at 3%.
analysis.headline: A wealth tax on roughly the richest few thousand households has 50 sponsors in the House, every one a Democrat, and has sat in the Ways and Means Committee without a markup or vote since it was referred in March 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new annual tax on the net value of everything a very rich household owns — stocks, businesses, property, art — not just what they sell in a year. Households would pay 2% on wealth above $50 million and 3% above $1 billion, and the top rate would double to 6% if Congress ever passes a universal government health insurance program. It also pays for beefed-up IRS enforcement to value and audit the largest fortunes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the new revenue reduces pressure on other taxes or funds public programs; the bill does not earmark its revenue, but it explicitly doubles its top rate to help pay for a universal health insurance program. Households below $50 million in net worth pay nothing. The IRS also gains a decade-long funding stream for enforcement, taxpayer services, and modernized systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone but the richest few thousand households

how_it_helps.text: The tax starts only at $50 million in net wealth (2%) and adds a 3% bracket above $1 billion, so no household below that threshold pays anything.

The top rate doubles from 3% to 6% in any year that legislation is in effect establishing comprehensive universal health insurance for all U.S. residents, explicitly tying the wealth tax to financing universal coverage.

Married couples are treated as one taxpayer, and property hidden in family trusts, gifts to young children, and expatriation schemes are attributed back to the wealthy individual, with a 40% rate applied to people who renounce citizenship to escape the tax.
The IRS must audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers every year, and new penalties of 30-50% apply to anyone who undervalues assets by large margins.
The bill authorizes $70 billion for IRS enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for systems modernization over fiscal years 2027 through 2037.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals (and married couples, counted jointly) with net wealth over $50 million — roughly the richest few thousand American households — plus multi-beneficiary trusts, which are taxed as if they were individuals. Wealthy owners of hard-to-value private companies face annual valuation of everything they own and penalties up to 50% for understatements.

drawbacks.text: Most billionaire wealth sits in private companies and other assets with no market price; the bill requires the Treasury to invent formulaic valuation methods within 12 months, which would almost certainly generate years of disputes and litigation over values.

Because the tax is on net value rather than cash income, some wealthy families would be billed on wealth they cannot easily sell; the bill itself anticipates this by letting the Treasury grant payment extensions of up to five years for severe liquidity problems or hardship to an ongoing business.

The bill applies a 40% rate to covered expatriates — people who give up U.S. citizenship — showing that wealthy individuals are expected to try leaving the tax system to avoid it, which could push some fortunes and investment offshore.
The revenue goes into the general fund rather than to any specific program; the only dedicated use contemplated is the higher 6% rate if a universal health program is enacted, which has not passed.

The plan leans on a ten-year, $100 billion IRS funding authorization to work; if future Congresses decline to appropriate the money, enforcement of a tax this dependent on valuation and auditing could fall short.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax falls on roughly the top few thousand households and leaves everyone below $50 million untouched, so the direct cost to ordinary people is nil and the revenue potential is large. The real question is administrability: annually valuing private companies, art, and trusts is genuinely hard, and the bill tries to solve that with new formulaic valuation rules, steep penalties, exit taxes, and a large IRS funding stream. Those design choices are serious but untested; whether they hold up in practice and litigation is the honest open risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since; Congress is still in session, so it is waiting.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2026 in the House on March 25, 2026, with 49 cosponsors listed on the bill, all Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Ways and Means, which handles all tax legislation, on the day of introduction.
The committee has held no markup, and the House has taken no further action on the bill since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything — the tax has not been enacted. Ultra-wealthy households continue to pay no federal tax on the accumulated value of their assets, and the bill's fate now rests with a committee controlled by the party with no cosponsors on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, holders of untaxed great wealth

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the wealth tax bill in the House.

for.name: 49 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including members of House leadership such as Rep. McGovern and prominent progressives such as Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Tlaib, and Pressley.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means (Republican-controlled)
against.role: Committee of referral for all tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no markup, no vote, no movement toward the floor.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican member signed on as a cosponsor, and the majority party controls the committee calendar that decides whether tax bills ever get a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican has signed on, in a House where tax legislation is controlled by a Republican-run Ways and Means Committee.

industries.industry: Ultra-high-net-worth households and billionaire family trusts
industries.note: The bill puts an annual federal tax on the total net value of their assets — 2% above $50 million, 3% above $1 billion — including wealth held in trusts and via gifts to minor children, with a 40% rate for people who renounce citizenship to avoid it. Its interest in the bill runs directly against the public's in the form of the revenue the tax would raise.

industries.industry: Private wealth management, trust, and estate-planning services
industries.note: Clients would face a new annual tax on everything they own and would need help restructuring trusts, valuing companies, and managing expatriation risk under the bill's 40% exit rate — a mix of lost client wealth and new paid work navigating the rules.

The bill requires the Treasury to build formulaic valuation methods for assets with no market price and obliges business entities to estimate their own value, creating a large market for valuation and compliance work; the fees would ultimately be borne by taxed families, not the public.

The bill authorizes $100 billion over eleven years — $70 billion for enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, $20 billion for modernization — plus a mandate to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers annually, reversing a decade of shrinking enforcement capacity aimed at the largest fortunes.

analysis.trajectory: With zero Republican cosponsors and the Ways and Means Committee in the opposing party's hands, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or a floor vote before this Congress ends, much like earlier versions of the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act in recent Congresses, which also died in committee without a vote.
